title: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
summary: How Megatron Core splits LLM training over thousands of GPUs: tensor, pipeline, sequence, context and expert parallelism, overlap, FP8, MFU, and planning, profiling and checkpointing a real run.
outcomes: Explain why Megatron splits the MLP column-wise then row-wise and compute TP traffic per layer as 8bsh(t-1)/t
Compute the pipeline bubble (p-1)/(vm), explain what 1F1B and interleaving fix, and rebalance uneven stages
Compute per-layer activation memory with TP, sequence parallelism and selective recompute
Explain Megatron's balanced causal CP split and choose a --cp-comm-type that fits the head layout and links
Trace an MoE layer's dispatch path, size its all-to-all traffic and explain MoE parallel folding
Pick an FP8 recipe for the hardware and say which tensors and collectives it changes
Compute MFU from tokens per second or logged TFLOP/s and tell it apart from hardware FLOPs utilization
Plan TP, PP, CP and DP for a cluster from memory and bubble estimates, then profile and checkpoint the run

lessons.title: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it

blocks.md:
Recall a training step from the prerequisites: a forward pass computes the loss, a backward pass computes a gradient for every weight, and the optimizer (usually Adam) updates the weights. Every step must keep the weights, their gradients and the optimizer state in GPU memory, plus the *activations*: tensors saved during the forward pass because the backward pass needs them.

Megatron Core (MCore) is NVIDIA's library, in the [NVIDIA/Megatron-LM](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM) repo, of GPU-optimized transformer building blocks and parallelism strategies for spreading this work over thousands of GPUs. This course explains each strategy, the formulas that predict its cost, and how to measure the result.

Start with memory. Large models train in *mixed precision*. The BF16 format (brain floating point, from Google Brain) is a 16-bit float with 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits; FP32 also has 8 exponent bits (same range) but 23 mantissa bits, so BF16 keeps only 2 to 3 significant digits. Matrix multiplies run fast in BF16, but the optimizer keeps an FP32 copy of every weight, because an update much smaller than the weight would be rounded away in BF16.

The Megatron Core distributed optimizer docs count the bytes each parameter needs with BF16 weights and FP32 gradients: 2 (BF16 weight) + 4 (FP32 gradient) + 4 (FP32 *main* copy of the weight that the optimizer updates) + 4 + 4 (Adam's two moment estimates: running averages of each weight's gradient and of its squared gradient, which set each step's size) = **18 bytes per parameter**.

For GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters that is 175e9 x 18 bytes = **3,150 GB**, before a single activation is stored. An A100 or H100 has 80 GB. Even ignoring activations, the model state alone needs at least 40 GPUs worth of memory.

blocks.title: Model state of GPT-3 175B (BF16 weights, FP32 grads, Adam)

scenes.caption: Each FP32 tensor costs 4 bytes x 175e9 = 700 GB; the BF16 weights cost 350 GB. Together 3,150 GB: about 39 times the 80 GB of one GPU.

blocks.md:
Compute is the second wall. Narayanan et al. (2021) estimate that training GPT-3 on a single V100 (the NVIDIA data-center GPU generation before the A100) would take about **288 years**. So we need many GPUs both to *fit* the model and to *finish* in weeks.

The simplest way to use many GPUs is *data parallelism* (DP): give every GPU a full copy of the model and a slice of the batch, then average the gradients with an *all-reduce*, a collective operation in which every GPU contributes a tensor and every GPU receives the elementwise sum (divided by the GPU count, that is the average). It solves the time problem only when the model fits on one GPU, and the paper notes two more limits: the per-GPU batch gets too small to keep the GPU busy, and you can never use more GPUs than there are samples in the batch.

Megatron splits the work along five axes. Each one cuts a different dimension of the computation:

- **Tensor parallelism (TP)**: split the weight matrices *inside* each layer across GPUs.
- **Pipeline parallelism (PP)**: give each GPU a contiguous slice of the layers, and feed the batch through in small pieces called *microbatches* (lesson 3) so the slices can work at the same time.
- **Data parallelism (DP)**: replicate the (already split) model and split the batch.
- **Context parallelism (CP)**: split the sequence (the tokens of one sample) across GPUs.
- **Expert parallelism (EP)**: in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, each layer's MLP is replaced by many smaller MLPs called *experts*, and a learned router sends each token to only a few of them; EP places different experts on different GPUs.

The combination of the first three is what the 2021 paper calls **PTD-P**: pipeline, tensor and data parallelism together. Tensor and pipeline parallelism are also called *model parallelism*, because they split the model itself rather than the data.

Two hardware words before the picture. Each GPU runs one process, and that process's integer id in the job (0, 1, 2, ...) is its *rank*. Inside one server, such as NVIDIA's DGX A100 with 8 A100 GPUs, the GPUs talk over **NVLink**, NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link (600 GB/s per A100). Between servers, traffic goes over **InfiniBand** network cards at 200 Gb/s, about 25 GB/s, each. That gap of more than ten times decides which axis may cross servers.

blocks.title: 8 GPUs as TP=2 x PP=2 x DP=2

scenes.caption: A 24-layer model on 8 GPUs. Each box is a tensor-parallel pair: two GPUs that together hold one copy of 12 layers, each GPU owning half of every weight matrix.
Pipeline parallelism: the first pair runs layers 1-12 and sends its output activations to the pair running layers 13-24. Point-to-point sends, once per microbatch.
Data parallelism: replica B holds the same weights as replica A but sees different samples. After the backward pass, matching shards average their gradients.
Megatron's default rank order is tp-cp-ep-dp-pp: TP varies fastest, so a TP group is consecutive ranks on one server, where the fast NVLink links are.

blocks.caption: The GPU count for the dense (non-expert) layers, as given in the Megatron Core context parallel docs. Mixture-of-experts layers regroup the same GPUs (lesson 7).

blocks.md: Every axis splits something different: TP splits matrices, PP splits layers, DP splits the batch, CP splits the sequence, EP splits experts. Choosing a configuration means choosing which communication you can afford on which link.

Scale adds one more constraint: failures. Meta's Llama 3 report describes a 54-day snapshot of pre-training its 405B model, which trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs. In that window the job was interrupted **466 times**: 47 planned interruptions (firmware upgrades, configuration or dataset changes) and 419 unexpected ones, about 78% of them confirmed or suspected hardware problems, with GPU issues the largest category at 58.7%. A single failed GPU can force the whole job to restart.

So a real configuration is judged by its restart cost as well as its speed: how often it checkpoints, how long a save and a reload take, and whether a checkpoint can be reloaded on a different number of GPUs. Lesson 10 shows how Megatron Core handles this.

blocks.question: A team has a 1.3B model (about 23 GB of model state at 18 bytes per parameter) that fits on one 80 GB GPU with its activations, and wants to train faster on 64 GPUs. Following the Megatron guidance, what should they try first?
options: TP=8 so every layer is split as finely as possible
Plain data parallelism (DP=64), adding model parallelism only if memory runs out
PP=64 so each GPU holds one or two layers
CP=64 so each GPU holds a sliver of each sequence
blocks.explain: The Megatron Core guide says to start with data parallelism and add TP, then PP, only when the model does not fit. Model parallelism adds communication and makes per-GPU matrix multiplies smaller, so it is a cost you pay for memory, not a free speedup.

blocks.question: Why does the 3,150 GB figure for GPT-3 175B not even include the largest memory user in many training runs?
options: It ignores the activations saved for the backward pass, which grow with batch size and sequence length
It ignores the tokenizer vocabulary
It counts Adam moments in BF16 instead of FP32
It forgets the gradients
blocks.explain: 18 bytes per parameter covers weights, gradients, main weights and Adam moments. Activations come on top and scale with microbatch size, sequence length and layer count. Lesson 4 is entirely about them.

lessons.title: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention

blocks.md:
The transformer MLP is two matrix multiplies (GEMMs) with a GeLU in between: $Y = \text{GeLU}(XA)$, then $Z = \text{Dropout}(YB)$. GeLU (Gaussian error linear unit) is a smooth version of ReLU: $\text{GeLU}(x) = x\,\Phi(x)$, where $\Phi(x)$ is the probability that a standard normal variable is below $x$. So GeLU(2) = 2 x 0.977 = 1.954 and GeLU(1) = 0.841. Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of values during training and stores a mask of which ones, so the backward pass can repeat it. Here $X$ has $h$ features per token, $A$ is $h \times 4h$ and $B$ is $4h \times h$.

Shoeybi et al. (2019) asked: how do we split $A$ and $B$ over $t$ GPUs so that each GPU does $1/t$ of the math and the GPUs talk as little as possible? There are two ways to cut a matrix, by rows or by columns, and the choice matters because GeLU is nonlinear.

blocks.prompt: Option 1: split $A$ by rows (and $X$ by columns), so GPU $i$ computes $X_i A_i$ and the true pre-activation is $X_1A_1 + X_2A_2$. Can each GPU apply GeLU to its own partial result and add afterwards?
blocks.reveal: No. GeLU of a sum is not the sum of the GeLUs, because GeLU is nonlinear. With the numbers in the next figure, the first output feature should be GeLU(1 + 1) = 1.954, but GeLU(1) + GeLU(1) = 1.683. A row split forces a synchronization (summing the partials) *before* the GeLU.

blocks.md:
Option 2: split $A$ by **columns**, $A = [A_1, A_2]$. Now each GPU holds the full input $X$ and computes complete pre-activations for its own half of the $4h$ features, so GeLU applies locally: $[Y_1, Y_2] = [\text{GeLU}(XA_1), \text{GeLU}(XA_2)]$. No communication.

The second GEMM is then split by **rows**, $B = [B_1; B_2]$, so GPU $i$ multiplies the $Y_i$ it already has: $YB = Y_1B_1 + Y_2B_2$. Each GPU now holds a *partial sum* of the output, and one all-reduce (sum across GPUs) produces $Z$.

blocks.title: One token through a 2-way tensor-parallel MLP

scenes.caption: Input token x = [1, 2] is replicated on both GPUs. A is 2 x 4 with columns (1, 0.5), (-1, 1), (0.5, -1), (2, -0.5).
Column split: GPU0 owns A's first two columns, GPU1 the last two. Pre-activations xA = [2, 1, -1.5, 1]; each GPU applies GeLU to its own two features with no communication.
Row split of B, whose rows are (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (-1, 0.5): GPU0 multiplies its y1 by the first two rows, GPU1 its y2 by the last two. Each result is a partial sum with the full output width.
The g operator (the paper's name for this all-reduce point) sums the partials: z = [1.013, 1.162] on both GPUs, exactly what one GPU computing the full MLP gets. One all-reduce for the whole MLP.

blocks.md:
Self-attention splits the same way, using the fact that heads are independent. The $Q$, $K$ and $V$ (query, key and value) projections are **column-parallel**: each GPU gets whole heads (with $t$-way TP, $a/t$ of the $a$ heads) and runs attention for them locally. The output projection is **row-parallel** and ends in one all-reduce.

So a full transformer layer needs two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass. The paper's names for the two communication points are $f$ and $g$:

- $f$ (before the column-parallel GEMM): identity forward, all-reduce of the input gradient backward.
- $g$ (after the row-parallel GEMM): all-reduce forward, identity backward.

blocks.caption: Abridged from megatron/core/tensor_parallel/mappings.py. The paper's f and g really are a few lines of PyTorch autograd.

blocks.md:
Why does $f$ all-reduce in the backward pass? Each GPU used the same $X$ but only its own columns of $A$, so each computes only part of $\partial L/\partial X$; the true gradient is the sum. $g$ mirrors it: summed outputs forward, and the gradient of a sum copies straight through.

The embedding is split too. The input embedding matrix is partitioned along the vocabulary, and so is the output layer, so GPU $r$ computes logits only for its own $v/t$ slice of the vocabulary. Gathering all the logits, the raw scores for each of the $v$ vocabulary entries at every token ($b \times s \times v$ values for $b$ sequences of $s$ tokens), would be enormous, so the loss is computed from the shards directly.

**Cross-entropy on a split vocabulary.** For one token with logits $z$ and target id $y$ the loss is $\log \sum_j e^{z_j} - z_y$, computed stably as $\log \sum_j e^{z_j - M} - (z_y - M)$ where $M$ is the largest logit. Megatron's `VocabParallelCrossEntropy` builds each piece from the shards:

1. Each GPU takes the max of its own logits; an all-reduce with MAX gives $M$.
2. Each GPU sums $e^{z_j - M}$ over its slice; an all-reduce with SUM gives the denominator.
3. Only the GPU that owns id $y$ has $z_y$. It contributes $z_y - M$, the others contribute 0, and an all-reduce with SUM delivers it everywhere.

That is three all-reduces of one number per token ($b \times s$ values each) instead of $b \times s \times v$ logits. The backward pass needs no communication: each GPU's gradient is the softmax on its slice minus 1 at the target, if it owns the target.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
z = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0, 3.0, 0.0, 1.5, -0.5])  # 1 token, v = 8
y = 6                                     # target id
shards = z.chunk(2)                       # GPU r owns ids 4r .. 4r+3
M = max(s.max() for s in shards)          # all-reduce MAX
sum_exp = sum(torch.exp(s - M).sum() for s in shards)   # all-reduce SUM
z_y = sum(s[y - 4*r] - M if 4*r <= y < 4*r + 4 else torch.tensor(0.)
          for r, s in enumerate(shards))  # all-reduce SUM, only the owner adds
loss = torch.log(sum_exp) - z_y
print([s.max().item() for s in shards], M.item())
print(round(sum_exp.item(), 4), z_y.item())
print(round(loss.item(), 4), round(F.cross_entropy(z[None], torch.tensor([y])).item(), 4))
# Output (run on CPU):
# [2.0, 3.0] 3.0
# 1.9067 -1.5
# 2.1454 2.1454
blocks.caption: Two simulated GPUs, vocabulary 8, one token, target id 6 (owned by GPU 1). The three reductions give the same loss as F.cross_entropy on the full logits. Run on CPU with PyTorch; the real kernel is in megatron/core/ops/loss/cross_entropy.py.

blocks.md: **Ring all-reduce, step by step.** Most all-reduces use a ring: the $t$ GPUs pass data to their neighbour in a circle, and the operation has two halves. In the **reduce-scatter**, each GPU cuts its tensor into $t$ pieces; for $t-1$ steps every GPU sends one piece ($1/t$ of the tensor) and adds the piece it receives, until each GPU holds the full sum of one piece. In the **all-gather**, the summed pieces travel around the ring for another $t-1$ steps until every GPU has all of them. Each half sends $(t-1)/t$ of the tensor per GPU, so a full all-reduce sends $2(t-1)/t$ of it, close to twice the tensor however many GPUs there are.

**How much does TP communicate?** Let $b$ be the microbatch size (the number of sequences in one forward pass; lesson 3 explains microbatches), $s$ the sequence length and $h$ the hidden size. Each all-reduce acts on a $b \times s \times h$ tensor, and a ring all-reduce over $t$ GPUs sends about $2(t-1)/t$ times the tensor size per GPU. Four all-reduces per layer (two forward, two backward) give the per-layer, per-microbatch volume from Narayanan et al.:

blocks.tex: V_{\text{TP}} = 8\,bsh\,\frac{t-1}{t} \;\text{elements per layer per GPU} \qquad V_{\text{PP}} = bsh \;\text{per stage boundary per direction}
blocks.caption: In words: 4 all-reduces x 2(t-1)/t x bsh gives 8bsh(t-1)/t elements per layer per GPU. Pipeline parallelism, by contrast, sends one bsh activation tensor between neighbouring stages (forward) and one gradient tensor back.

blocks.md:
Worked example, GPT-3 175B ($s = 2048$, $h = 12288$, $b = 1$, BF16 so 2 bytes per element, $t = 8$):

- One all-reduce payload: $bsh$ = 25.2M elements = **50 MB**.
- TP per layer: $8 \cdot bsh \cdot 7/8$ = 176M elements = **352 MB** per microbatch.
- With 96 layers on 8 pipeline stages (12 layers each), every GPU moves about **4.2 GB** of TP traffic per microbatch.
- The pipeline sends 50 MB per stage boundary per direction, and only **6.3 MB** per GPU with the paper's scatter/gather trick (each of the 8 TP ranks sends 1/8 over its own InfiniBand card, then they all-gather over NVLink).

blocks.title: TP traffic vs pipeline traffic per microbatch (units of bsh)

y.label: elements sent per GPU, in units of bsh

scenes.caption: Per layer, TP traffic approaches 8 bsh as t grows; it does not shrink with more GPUs. A 12-layer stage at t = 8 moves 84 bsh per microbatch, versus 2 bsh for the pipeline.
With only 2 layers per stage, TP traffic is still 14 bsh at t = 8. Pipeline sends are point-to-point and small, which is why PP is the axis that crosses slow inter-node links.

blocks.md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

blocks.question: In a 2-way TP MLP, an engineer splits the first weight matrix A by rows instead of columns, keeping everything else the same. What breaks?
options: Nothing, matrix multiplication is linear so the split does not matter
GeLU is applied to partial sums, so outputs are wrong unless an extra all-reduce is inserted before the GeLU
The backward pass needs twice as much memory
The second GEMM can no longer be split
blocks.explain: A row split of A gives each GPU a partial pre-activation. GeLU is nonlinear, so GeLU of the parts does not add up to GeLU of the whole (1.683 vs 1.954 in the example). The column split avoids this synchronization entirely.

blocks.question: For a fixed model, a team doubles TP from 4 to 8 inside a server. Per GPU and per layer, how does TP communication volume change?
options: It halves, because each GPU holds half as many weights
It stays the same
It grows from 6 bsh to 7 bsh, about 17% more
It doubles
blocks.explain: Volume is 8bsh(t-1)/t: 8 x 3/4 = 6 bsh at t = 4 and 8 x 7/8 = 7 bsh at t = 8. Communication does not shrink with more TP ranks while compute per GPU halves, so the communication share of each step rises.

blocks.question: With TP = 8 and a 128,000-token vocabulary, what does the vocabulary-parallel loss move between the 8 GPUs for each token in the forward pass?
options: All 128,000 logits, gathered onto every GPU
The 16,000 logits of each GPU's slice, sent to GPU 0
Nothing, each GPU computes its own loss on its slice
Three scalars through all-reduces: the max, the sum of exponentials and the target logit
blocks.explain: The max (MAX all-reduce), the sum of exponentials (SUM) and the target logit from its owner (SUM) are enough to form log sum exp minus the target logit. A per-slice loss would be wrong, because softmax normalizes over the whole vocabulary.

lessons.title: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule

blocks.md:
Pipeline parallelism gives each of $p$ devices a contiguous slice of layers: a *stage*. A single sample would leave all but one stage idle, so the batch is cut into $m$ **microbatches** that flow through the stages one after another, like cars on an assembly line.

Megatron keeps *strict optimizer semantics*: every microbatch's forward and backward pass uses the same weights, and the optimizer steps once at the end of the batch. That requires a **pipeline flush**: all microbatches must drain before the update. Devices idle while the pipeline fills and drains, and this idle time is the **pipeline bubble**.

The figure compares three schedules. GPipe (Huang et al., 2019, from Google) runs every forward pass before any backward pass. **1F1B**, short for one forward, one backward, comes from Narayanan et al.'s PipeDream work; PipeDream-Flush is its variant with a pipeline flush, and it alternates forwards and backwards.

blocks.title: Three schedules for p = 4 devices and m = 8 microbatches

scenes.caption: GPipe: all forwards (blue, 1 unit) then all backwards (2 units). Simplified: no communication time. The ideal is 8 x 3 = 24 units (marker), but the flush ends at 33.
1F1B (PipeDream-Flush): after a short warm-up, each device alternates one forward and one backward. Still 33 units: the bubble is identical. What changes is memory (next figure).
Interleaved 1F1B with v = 2 chunks per device: device 1 runs stages 1 and 5, device 2 stages 2 and 6, and so on. Each chunk is half the work, so fill and drain shrink: done at 28.5.

blocks.md: Count the bubble in the GPipe picture. Device 4 cannot start until $p-1$ forward passes have happened upstream, and device 1 waits through $p-1$ backward passes at the end. With per-microbatch forward and backward times $t_f$ and $t_b$, the bubble is $(p-1)(t_f + t_b)$, while the useful work is $m(t_f + t_b)$. For the figure: $3 \times 3 = 9$ idle units against 24 ideal, so the flush ends at 33.

blocks.caption: From Narayanan et al. (2021): bubble time (p-1)(t_f + t_b) over ideal time m(t_f + t_b); t_f + t_b cancels, leaving (p-1)/m. With v chunks per device each chunk takes t_f / v and t_b / v, so fill and drain shrink v times.

blocks.md:
**1F1B fixes memory, not the bubble.** GPipe runs all $m$ forwards before any backward, so every device stashes activations for all $m$ microbatches. In 1F1B, device $d$ (counting from 0) does only $p - d - 1$ warm-up forwards, then strictly alternates one forward and one backward, so a device never holds more than $p$ microbatches in flight. When $m \gg p$ that is a large saving, and it is the schedule Megatron uses.

**Interleaving attacks the bubble.** Instead of device 1 owning layers 1-4 of a 16-layer model, it owns layers 1-2 and 9-10 (two *model chunks*), device 2 owns 3-4 and 11-12, and so on. Megatron calls these *virtual pipeline stages*. The cost: $v$ times more point-to-point sends. The paper's schedule needs $m$ to be a multiple of $p$. Megatron Core runs microbatches in groups of $N$ per virtual stage (`--microbatch-group-size-per-virtual-pipeline-stage`, default $N = p$) and stops with an error unless $p \le N \le m$ and the last group is full or holds at least $p$ microbatches. With the default, $m$ must still be a multiple of $p$.

blocks.title: Peak microbatches of activations held per device

scenes.caption: GPipe: every device stores activations for all 8 microbatches before its first backward pass.
1F1B: device d holds at most p - d microbatches (4, 3, 2, 1). Device 1 holds the most: p microbatches of L/p layers each (L is the total layer count), a full model's worth of layer activations.
Interleaved (v = 2), measured in full-stage units: 5.5, 4.5, 3.5, 2.5. Device 1 holds 1 + (p-1)/(pv) = 1.375 times the 1F1B amount, matching Korthikanti et al. (lesson 4).

blocks.title: Bubble vs number of microbatches

scenes.caption: p = 4, v = 1: at m = 8 the bubble is 3/8 = 37.5% of ideal time (27% of the whole step). You need m much larger than p.
Interleaving with v = 2 halves it: 3/16 = 18.75% at m = 8, as in the timeline.
p = 8 at m = 32 gives 7/32 = 21.9%; with v = 4 it drops to 5.5%. Deep pipelines need many microbatches or interleaving.

blocks.prompt: The global batch is fixed. A team doubles the microbatch size $b$ to make each GEMM bigger and more efficient. What happens to the bubble?
blocks.reveal: It grows. With global batch $B$ and data-parallel size $d$, the number of microbatches is $m = B/(b \cdot d)$, so doubling $b$ halves $m$ and doubles $(p-1)/m$. Narayanan et al. show the two effects fight: larger microbatches raise per-GPU efficiency (up to 1.3x on one GPU in their Figure 7) but enlarge the bubble, so the best $b$ is model dependent (4 for one model, 2 for their 91B config).

blocks.md: In Megatron, interleaving is set with `--num-layers-per-virtual-pipeline-stage`. The MoE guide notes that the valid values divide num_layers / PP and that larger v means fewer bubbles but more point-to-point traffic, so a middle value is often best.

**Uneven stages.** The bubble formula assumes every stage takes the same time. Real models are not even: the first stage also runs the input embedding, and the last stage runs the output layer (the logits GEMM over the whole vocabulary) and the loss. For Llama 3 405B (hidden size 16,384, 128,000-token vocabulary) the logits GEMM has 16,384 x 128,000 = 2.10B weights, while one transformer layer has 3.19B, so the last stage carries about two thirds of an extra layer of GEMM work.

In steady state 1F1B moves at the pace of the slowest stage, so a heavy stage slows everyone. A simulation of the schedule (p = 4, m = 8, forward 1 unit, backward 2) with the last stage 10% slower stretches the step from 33 to 35.4 units, 7.3% longer. The time is about $m(t_f + t_b)_{\max} + (p-1)(t_f + t_b)$, so unlike the bubble this loss does not shrink with more microbatches: at m = 64 it is 9.6%.

blocks.title: Busy share of each stage: balanced vs last stage 10% heavier

scenes.caption: Balanced, p = 4, m = 8: every stage computes 24 of 33 units (72.7%). The other 27.3% is the ordinary bubble.
Last stage 10% heavier (simulated 1F1B): the step takes 35.4 units. Stages 1 to 3 still do 24 units, so they are busy only 67.8%; stage 4 is busy 74.6%.

blocks.md: The fix is to give the heavy stages fewer transformer layers. Llama 3 removed one layer each from its first and last stages. Megatron Core offers three knobs: `--decoder-first-pipeline-num-layers` and `--decoder-last-pipeline-num-layers` set those stages' layer counts directly; `--account-for-embedding-in-pipeline-split` and `--account-for-loss-in-pipeline-split` count the embedding or the loss as one layer when splitting; and the experimental `--pipeline-model-parallel-layout` takes a string such as `"Et*3|(tt|)*29,m|L"` (E embedding, t transformer layer, m multi-token-prediction layer, L loss, stages split by |), the docs' example for a DeepSeek-V3-style stack on 16 stages with 2 virtual stages each.
Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

blocks.question: p = 8 pipeline stages, m = 32 microbatches, interleaved with v = 4 chunks per device. What is the bubble as a fraction of ideal time?
blocks.explain: (p - 1) / (v m) = 7 / (4 x 32) = 7/128 = 5.5%. Without interleaving it would be 7/32 = 21.9%.

blocks.question: Why did Megatron adopt 1F1B (PipeDream-Flush) over GPipe even though both have the same bubble?
options: 1F1B needs no pipeline flush
1F1B sends fewer bytes between stages
1F1B caps in-flight microbatches at p instead of m, so activation memory stops growing with the number of microbatches
1F1B lets each microbatch use slightly stale weights, which is faster
blocks.explain: The bubble is (p-1)/m for both. GPipe stores activations for all m microbatches; 1F1B starts backward passes early and never has more than p outstanding. This is what makes a large m (small bubble) affordable.

blocks.question: A 4-stage pipeline's last stage is 10% slower than the others because of the logits and loss. The team raises m from 8 to 64 microbatches. What happens to the slowdown caused by the heavy stage?
options: It disappears, like the bubble, once m is much larger than p
It grows slightly, from 7.3% to about 9.6%, because every microbatch waits for the slow stage
It shrinks from 7.3% to under 1%
It doubles, because the last stage holds more activations
blocks.explain: The step is about m(t_f + t_b) of the slowest stage plus a fill and drain term. The fill and drain share shrinks with m but the per-microbatch penalty does not, so the slowdown approaches the full 10%. Only rebalancing layers removes it.

lessons.title: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP

blocks.md:
After TP and PP split the weights, activations become the memory problem. Korthikanti et al. (2022) count, for one transformer layer in 16-bit, the bytes saved for the backward pass ($a$ = attention heads):

- Attention block: $11sbh + 5as^2b$. The $s^2$ terms are the softmax output, its dropout mask and the dropout output: one $s \times s$ matrix per head.
- MLP: $19sbh$ (inputs of both GEMMs, the GeLU input of width $4h$, a dropout mask).
- Two layer norms: $4sbh$.

blocks.caption: Adding the parts: 11 + 19 + 4 = 34 sbh, and 5as-squared-b equals sbh x 5as/h. This is Equation 1 of Korthikanti et al. For GPT-3 (a = 96, s = 2048, h = 12288) 5as/h = 80, so the attention-score term is more than twice the rest.

blocks.md:
Tensor parallelism splits the activations *inside* the attention and MLP blocks, but not the layer norms, the dropouts after each block, or the inputs to the blocks. These are replicated on all $t$ GPUs: $10sbh$ (4 for the two layer-norm inputs, 2 for the two dropout masks, 4 for the inputs of the attention and MLP blocks) that does not shrink with $t$. The other $24sbh$ and the attention-score term are split $t$ ways. Per layer, TP gives $sbh(10 + 24/t + 5as/(ht))$.

**Sequence parallelism (SP)** observes that layer norm and dropout act on each token independently, so those regions can be split along the *sequence* dimension. Each of the $t$ GPUs keeps $s/t$ of the tokens there. The TP all-reduce is replaced by its two halves: an **all-gather** entering the TP region and a **reduce-scatter** leaving it.

blocks.title: One MLP block with TP = 2 plus sequence parallelism

scenes.caption: Sequence-parallel region: each GPU runs layer norm on its own half of the tokens (s/2 x b x h). Nothing is replicated.
Operator g, forward: all-gather along the sequence. Each GPU now has the full Y it needs as input to the column-parallel GEMM.
Tensor-parallel region: GEMM with A's columns, GeLU, GEMM with B's rows, exactly as in lesson 2. Each GPU ends with a partial sum W_i of the full output.
Operator g-bar, forward: reduce-scatter. Partials are summed and each GPU keeps only its own tokens, ready for the sequence-split dropout.
Backward swaps the roles: g-bar becomes an all-gather of gradients and g a reduce-scatter. Every collective has a conjugate.

blocks.md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

**Activation recomputation** (also called checkpointing) means not saving some activations in the forward pass and recomputing them from saved inputs during the backward pass: it trades extra compute for memory. *Full* recompute does this for the whole layer, keeping only the layer's input. *Selective* recompute does it only for a few chosen tensors.

**Selective activation recomputation.** The $5as/h$ term comes from attention scores, softmax and its dropout: huge tensors (quadratic in $s$) with very few FLOPs per element. Recomputing *only those* in the backward pass, instead of the whole layer, removes the term at little cost.

For GPT-3 the recomputed part is $4bs^2h$ extra FLOPs per layer (the $QK^T$ and attention-over-$V$ GEMMs, each $2bs^2h$ because a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs). The layer's other GEMMs cost $24bsh^2$: $6bsh^2$ for the query, key and value projections, $2bsh^2$ for the output projection and $16bsh^2$ for the two MLP GEMMs. Dividing, $4bs^2h/(24bsh^2 + 4bs^2h) = 4s/(24h + 4s)$ = **2.7%** of the forward FLOPs (the paper's figure), or 0.9% of a full forward plus backward step. In exchange it saves $80/114$ = **70%** of the activation memory.

blocks.title: GPT-3 175B: activation memory per layer (t = 8, b = 1)

scenes.caption: One layer on one GPU with no splitting: sbh(34 + 80) = 2.87 GB. Times 96 layers that is 275 GB.
TP = 8 cuts it to 0.58 GB. But the replicated 10 sbh (layer norms, dropouts, block inputs) is 0.25 GB of that, 43% of what is left, and it never shrinks with t.
Adding SP (0.36 GB) or selective recompute (0.33 GB) each nearly halves the TP figure. Together: 34 sbh / t = 0.107 GB, 18.5% of TP alone: the paper's 5x reduction.
Full recompute stores only each layer's input, 2 sbh = 0.050 GB, but reruns the whole forward pass (30 to 40% time overhead in the paper). SP + selective gets within about 2x of it for about 4%.

blocks.md:
Now multiply by layers. With 1F1B, pipeline stage 1 holds $p$ microbatches of $L/p$ layers each, so it stores **$L$ layers worth** of activations regardless of $p$ (lesson 3). For GPT-3 with TP = 8, SP and selective recompute: 96 x 0.107 GB = **10.3 GB** on the first stage; with interleaving ($p = 8$, $v = 3$) multiply by $1 + (p-1)/(pv) = 1.29$ to get **13.3 GB**. With TP alone it would be 55.6 GB; the paper reports that with TP alone and no recompute, every one of its test models (22B to 1T) needs more than the 80 GB of an A100.

Measured on a 22B layer, full recompute added 39% to the layer's forward plus backward time; SP plus selective recompute added 4%.

The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022, which computes attention tile by tile in fast on-chip memory; also in NVIDIA's Transformer Engine library) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

**Context parallelism (CP)** goes further than SP: it splits *all* activations, including attention, along the sequence. Linear layers and norms work per token, so they need no change. Attention does need every earlier key and value, so the GPUs of a CP group exchange key-value (KV) chunks. The guide recommends CP for sequences of 8K tokens and longer, and suggests it in place of larger TP when long sequences cause out-of-memory errors. Lesson 5 shows how Megatron splits the sequence, keeps the work balanced under a causal mask, and chooses how to move the KV chunks.

blocks.question: A model has 5as/h = 20 (short sequences, wide hidden size). Compared with GPT-3 (5as/h = 80), how much does selective recompute help it?
options: Exactly as much, it always saves 70%
More: it removes 80% because the model is wider
Nothing, selective recompute only works with sequence parallelism
Less: it removes 20/54 = 37% of activation memory
blocks.explain: Selective recompute removes the 5as/h part of 34 + 5as/h. For 5as/h = 20 that is 20/54 = 37%. The trick shines for long sequences and many heads, where the quadratic attention term dominates.

blocks.question: Why does sequence parallelism not increase communication over plain TP?
options: It compresses activations before sending them
It skips the backward-pass communication
An all-reduce is a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, and SP issues exactly those two halves at different points
It sends activations only between pipeline stages
blocks.explain: TP does 4 all-reduces per layer per step; TP + SP does 4 all-gathers and 4 reduce-scatters. A ring all-reduce is implemented as reduce-scatter then all-gather, so the bandwidth used is the same. The paper even measured a small speedup from running layer norm and dropout on 1/t of the data.

lessons.title: Context parallelism: balanced causal splits and the KV ring

blocks.md:
Take a sequence of 8 tokens and two GPUs, so CP = 2. Every layer except attention treats tokens independently, so each GPU can run the norms and linear layers on its own 4 tokens and store only their activations. Attention is the exception: a query must see the keys and values of all earlier tokens, wherever they live. The Megatron Core docs describe CP as exactly this: inputs and all activations split along the sequence, plus an exchange of KV chunks for attention.

CP sits in the GPU count $\text{TP} \times \text{CP} \times \text{PP} \times \text{DP}$ next to the other axes. A CP group is the set of GPUs that hold different pieces of the same sequences: with TP = 2 and CP = 2 on 4 GPUs, GPUs 0 and 2 exchange KV, and so do GPUs 1 and 3. Because all GPUs in a CP group hold the same weights, their gradients are summed together with the data-parallel ones.

Two ideas from the *Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention* course (outside this course's prerequisites; its lessons 4 and 5 go deeper) are used here, so in brief. **Online softmax**: attention for one query can be computed one KV block at a time by keeping a running max $m$ of the scores, a running sum $l$ of $e^{\text{score} - m}$ and a running weighted sum $o$ of values; when a block raises the max, the old $l$ and $o$ are multiplied by $e^{m_{\text{old}} - m_{\text{new}}}$, and at the end $o / l$ is exact attention in any block order. **Ring Attention** passes KV blocks around a ring of GPUs while each computes on the block it holds. This lesson is about how Megatron Core applies them: which tokens each GPU gets, what one ring step costs, and the four communication types it offers.

blocks.prompt: Split the 8 tokens contiguously: GPU 0 gets tokens 0-3, GPU 1 gets tokens 4-7. Under a causal mask token $i$ attends to $i + 1$ keys. How many query-key scores does each GPU compute?
blocks.reveal: GPU 0: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = **10**. GPU 1: 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = **26**, 2.6 times as many. For long sequences the ratio approaches 3 (the second half of a causal triangle has three times the area of the first). The ring advances in lockstep, so GPU 0 idles most of the time.

blocks.title: Causal attention work on CP = 2, 8 tokens (1 = GPU 0, 2 = GPU 1)

scenes.caption: Each cell is one query-key score that must be computed; 0 means masked (the key is in the future). Contiguous split: GPU 0 owns queries 0-3 and computes 10 scores.
GPU 1 owns queries 4-7 and computes 26 scores, 2.6 times as many. As sequences grow the ratio tends to 3, and the whole ring waits for GPU 1.
Megatron's split: 4 chunks of 2 tokens. GPU 0 takes chunks 0 and 3 (tokens 0, 1, 6, 7), GPU 1 takes chunks 1 and 2 (tokens 2-5). Each computes exactly 18 scores.
Off-diagonal work is also halved evenly: GPU 0's queries meet GPU 1's keys in 8 cells (rows 6-7, columns 2-5), exactly half of the 4 x 4 block.

blocks.md:
Megatron cuts the sequence into $2 \times \text{CP}$ chunks and gives rank $i$ chunks $i$ and $2\,\text{CP} - 1 - i$, an early chunk and the matching late one (`get_batch_on_this_cp_rank` in Megatron Core; Llama 3 used the same assignment). For CP = 2 that is chunks (0, 3) and (1, 2), 18 scores each. The sequence length must be divisible by $2 \times \text{CP}$.

The split also balances every ring step. On the diagonal step a GPU attends its own two chunks; on every other step it meets one other GPU's chunks and exactly half of that block is unmasked, so all GPUs do equal work at every step. The docs credit this, plus using cuDNN (NVIDIA's library of tuned deep-learning kernels) and open-source flash attention kernels, for Megatron's CP being faster than plain Ring Attention.

blocks.title: The p2p ring with CP = 4 (one layer, forward pass)

scenes.caption: Step 0: every GPU computes attention of its own queries against its own KV chunk (the diagonal blocks) and, at the same time, sends that KV chunk to the next GPU.
Step 1: each GPU computes on the chunk it just received, merging the partial result into its running max, sum and output, and forwards the chunk.
Step 2 sends the last chunk each GPU still needs; step 3 computes on it with no further send. After CP - 1 = 3 transfers every query has met every key, and the result is exact.

Backward: each GPU kept only its own KV chunk, so the chunks travel the ring again, and the partial KV gradients computed on every GPU are summed back to each chunk's owner: the docs' reduce-scatter of KV gradients.

blocks.code:
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0); S, D, CP = 8, 4, 2
q, k, v = (torch.randn(S, D) for _ in range(3))
causal = torch.triu(torch.ones(S, S, dtype=torch.bool), 1)
ref = torch.softmax((q @ k.T / D**0.5).masked_fill(causal, -1e9), -1) @ v
c = S // (2 * CP)                       # 2*CP chunks; rank r gets r and 2CP-1-r
pos = [torch.cat([torch.arange(r*c, r*c+c), torch.arange((2*CP-1-r)*c, (2*CP-r)*c)])
       for r in range(CP)]
out = torch.zeros(S, D)
for r in range(CP):
    qp = pos[r]; m = torch.full((2*c,), -1e9); l = torch.zeros(2*c); o = torch.zeros(2*c, D)
    for step in range(CP):              # ring: KV chunk of rank r-step arrives
        kp = pos[(r - step) % CP]
        mask = kp[None] > qp[:, None]
        s = (q[qp] @ k[kp].T / D**0.5).masked_fill(mask, -1e9)
        m2 = torch.maximum(m, s.max(-1).values); a = torch.exp(m - m2)
        p = torch.exp(s - m2[:, None]).masked_fill(mask, 0)
        l = l * a + p.sum(-1); o = o * a[:, None] + p @ v[kp]; m = m2
        print(f"rank {r} step {step}: {int((~mask).sum())} score pairs")
    out[qp] = o / l[:, None]
print("tokens:", [p.tolist() for p in pos])
print("max |CP - full| =", f"{(out - ref).abs().max().item():.1e}")
# Output (run on CPU):
# rank 0 step 0: 10 score pairs
# rank 0 step 1: 8 score pairs
# rank 1 step 0: 10 score pairs
# rank 1 step 1: 8 score pairs
# tokens: [[0, 1, 6, 7], [2, 3, 4, 5]]
# max |CP - full| = 1.2e-07
blocks.caption: CP = 2 simulated on one CPU with PyTorch: balanced chunks, a 2-step ring and the online-softmax merge reproduce full causal attention to float rounding, with 10 + 8 = 18 scores per rank. Real CP runs this inside Transformer Engine's attention on GPUs.

blocks.md: **When does the ring hide its traffic?** Let $c = s/\text{CP}$ be the tokens per GPU, $H$ the query heads, $H_{kv}$ the KV heads, $d$ the head size, $F$ the GPU's FLOP/s and $B$ the link's bytes per second. An off-diagonal step computes half of a $c \times c$ block, $2c^2Hd$ FLOPs (the $QK^T$ and weights-times-$V$ products cost $2c^2Hd$ each for a full block). Meanwhile the GPU sends its K and V chunks in BF16: $2 \times c \times H_{kv} d \times 2 = 4cH_{kv}d$ bytes. The send is hidden when compute takes longer:

blocks.caption: Compute grows with c squared and traffic with c, so long sequences always win. Grouped-query attention helps directly: with 8 KV heads for 64 query heads (Llama 3 70B's layout) the KV chunk is 8 times smaller than with full multi-head attention.

blocks.title: One ring step: attention compute vs KV transfer (H100, 64 heads)

x.label: tokens per GPU c = s / CP

scenes.caption: 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention) over a 25 GB/s link: the transfer hides once each GPU holds about 9,900 tokens. Compute grows as c squared, transfer only as c.
Same link with 64 KV heads (no GQA): the KV chunk is 8 times larger and the break-even moves to about 79,000 tokens per GPU.
Inside a server at an assumed 400 GB/s, 8 KV heads hide behind compute from about 620 tokens per GPU. Simplified: peak FLOP/s, forward only, no kernel overheads.

blocks.md: Worked numbers from the formula, for 64 query heads of size 128 and 8 KV heads at the H100's dense BF16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s (the spec sheet's 1,979 is with sparsity): a 32K sequence on CP = 4 gives $c$ = 8,192 tokens per GPU. One step computes $1.10 \times 10^{12}$ FLOPs, 1.11 ms at peak, and sends a 33.6 MB KV chunk: 1.34 ms at 25 GB/s (exposed) but 0.08 ms at 400 GB/s (hidden). This fits the parallelism guide's advice to use CP for sequences of 8K tokens and longer, and is why CP groups prefer fast links.

**Four ways to move KV.** `--cp-comm-type` chooses, and it can be set per layer (`--cp-comm-type p2p p2p a2a ...`):

- `p2p` (default): the ring above. Sends are asynchronous and overlap attention compute.
- `allgather`: gather all K and V before attention, as Llama 3 did. Simple and flexible for unusual masks, but not overlapped.
- `a2a`: like DeepSpeed Ulysses, an all-to-all regroups Q, K and V so each GPU holds the full sequence for a subset of heads.
- `a2a+p2p`: hierarchical. All-to-all inside a low-level group (for example over NVLink) and the p2p ring across groups (for example over InfiniBand); the group sizes come from `--hierarchical-context-parallel-sizes`.

`a2a` splits heads, so Transformer Engine requires the number of query heads **and** of KV heads on each GPU to be divisible by CP. TP has already divided the heads: with 8 KV heads and TP = 4 each GPU holds 2, so a2a works for CP = 2 but is rejected for CP = 4. The p2p ring has no head constraint, which is one reason it is the default.

CP versus more TP: TP's per-layer all-reduce volume stays near $8bsh$ however large $t$ gets (lesson 2), while CP divides both the attention compute and the KV traffic per GPU by CP and moves only K and V, which grouped-query attention makes small. The docs' Figure 2 shows GPT 175B runs combining TP and CP beating full recomputation, which costs about 30%. With the distributed optimizer, the optimizer state is also sharded across the CP ranks (lesson 6).

CP splits every activation along the sequence. Megatron balances causal work by giving rank i chunks i and 2CP - 1 - i, and hides the KV ring when each GPU holds enough tokens: c at least 2(H_kv / H)(F / B).

blocks.question: A model has 64 query heads and 8 KV heads and trains with TP = 4 and CP = 4 at 32K tokens. Which `--cp-comm-type` will Transformer Engine reject?
options: a2a, because each GPU holds only 2 KV heads and 2 is not divisible by CP = 4
p2p, because the ring needs the sequence to be divisible by 64
allgather, because it cannot be combined with TP
None of them; any type works with grouped-query attention
blocks.explain: a2a scatters heads across the CP group, so the per-GPU query heads (64 / 4 = 16) and KV heads (8 / 4 = 2) must both be divisible by CP. 2 is not divisible by 4. p2p only needs the sequence divisible by 2 x CP = 8; a2a+p2p with an a2a group of 2 would also work.

blocks.question: A CP group is moved from NVLink inside one server to GPUs on different servers, and the ring's KV transfers become exposed. Which change most directly hides them again?
options: Raise CP so each GPU holds fewer tokens and sends smaller chunks
Switch from grouped-query to multi-head attention
Use contiguous chunks instead of the 2 x CP split
Lower CP so each GPU holds more tokens, since compute grows as c squared and traffic only as c
blocks.explain: The break-even is c at least 2(H_kv/H)(F/B). A slower link raises it, so each GPU needs more tokens: a smaller CP (or longer sequences). Raising CP shrinks compute faster than traffic. More KV heads makes the chunk bigger, and contiguous chunks unbalance the ring.

lessons.title: Distributed optimizer and hiding communication behind compute

blocks.md:
Back to the 18 bytes per parameter from lesson 1. Plain DP replicates all of it on every data-parallel rank. Megatron Core's **distributed optimizer** shards the optimizer part across the $d$ data-parallel ranks, as in ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer, Rajbhandari et al., 2020, from Microsoft's DeepSpeed team; ZeRO stage 1 shards optimizer state, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also the weights): each rank keeps FP32 main weights and Adam moments for only $1/d$ of the parameters.

The docs give the per-parameter cost (BF16 weights, FP32 gradients) as $6 + 12/d$ bytes: 2 for the weight and 4 for the gradient buffer are kept everywhere, 12 bytes of optimizer state are sharded.

blocks.title: Distributed optimizer step on 4 data-parallel ranks

scenes.caption: Backward pass done: each rank holds local gradients for all 16 elements, computed from its own slice of the batch.
Reduce-scatter: rank 0 now holds the fully summed gradient for elements 0-3, rank 1 for 4-7, and so on. The other 12 slots on each rank are stale.
optimizer.step(): each rank updates only its 4 FP32 main weights (it owns only those Adam moments) and casts them to BF16 parameters.
All-gather: every rank receives the other 12 updated BF16 parameters and can start the next forward pass. Reduce-scatter plus all-gather moves the same number of elements as one gradient all-reduce.

blocks.title: Bytes per parameter vs data-parallel size
blocks.caption: BF16 weights, FP32 gradients. At d = 8 the cost is 7.5 bytes, at d = 64 6.19 bytes: GPT-3's state drops from 3,150 GB to about 1,083 GB per model copy.

scenes.caption: At d = 8 the distributed optimizer needs 7.5 bytes per parameter instead of 18; it approaches 6 as d grows. Megatron-FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) goes further and also shards gradients and weights (ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3 style).

blocks.md:
**Why the last layers' gradients are ready first.** The backward pass runs from the last layer to the first, so layer $L$'s weight gradients are final while layer 1's have not started. Megatron Core's data-parallel wrapper lays the gradient buffer out in that backprop order and cuts it into **buckets**: by default at most max(40M, 1M x DP size) parameters each, larger at large DP so that each collective is not dominated by latency.

With `--overlap-grad-reduce`, a bucket's reduce-scatter (an all-reduce without the distributed optimizer) is launched asynchronously the moment every parameter in it has its gradient, while backward continues on earlier layers. With several microbatches, buckets are marked ready only on the **last** microbatch; earlier ones just accumulate into the buffer, since sending a partial sum would waste bandwidth.

**Why parameters can be prefetched.** After the optimizer step each rank holds updated weights only for its own shard, so the next forward pass needs an all-gather of the BF16 weights. Layer order is known in advance, so `--overlap-param-gather` launches the next bucket's all-gather when the current bucket is waited on: layer $i+1$'s weights travel while layer $i$ computes. `--overlap-param-gather-with-optimizer-step` also overlaps the first bucket's gather with the optimizer step itself.

blocks.title: Gradient buckets and parameter prefetch, 4 layers (simplified)

scenes.caption: Backward without overlap: layers run last to first (2 units each), then the four bucket reduce-scatters (1.5 units each) run back to back. The step ends at 14.
--overlap-grad-reduce: layer 4's bucket is complete at t = 2, so its reduce-scatter starts while layer 3 computes. Only the last bucket is exposed: done at 9.5.
Forward without overlap: the distributed optimizer must all-gather each layer's updated BF16 weights (0.75 units) before the forward pass uses them. Forward ends at 7.
--overlap-param-gather: when layer 1 waits on its gather, layer 2's gather is launched, and so on, so each layer's weights arrive while the previous layer computes. Forward ends at 4.75.

blocks.md: **Tensor-parallel overlap.** TP's collectives sit *on* the critical path: the column-parallel GEMM cannot start without the all-gathered input. `--tp-comm-overlap` (needs TP of at least 2 and `--sequence-parallel`) uses two tricks from Transformer Engine. *Bulk* overlap runs a collective alongside a GEMM that does not depend on it. *Pipelined* overlap splits the dependent all-gather or reduce-scatter into chunks, so the GEMM works on chunk $i$ while chunk $i+1$ is in flight. Pipeline sends and receives are overlapped automatically in the 1F1B phase when virtual pipeline stages are on (the `overlap_p2p_comm` setting, on by default; `--no-overlap-p2p-communication` turns it off).

**Megatron-FSDP, the ZeRO-3 option.** `--use-megatron-fsdp` with `--data-parallel-sharding-strategy optim_grads_params` also shards the BF16 weights and gradients (`optim` and `optim_grads` are the ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 levels), approaching zero model state per GPU as DP grows instead of 6 bytes per parameter. The price is communication: each layer's weights are gathered just before use, and fully sharded schemes gather them again for the backward pass (Llama 3's report skips that reshard to avoid the extra all-gather). The guide recommends it for large models with large or fused kernels that can hide the traffic. The MoE Parallel Folding paper measured plain FSDP below 10% MFU on MoE models, where sparse compute leaves little to hide it under.

Overlap works because each collective has slack: gradients of late layers are ready early, and weights of the next layer are known before they are needed. What remains exposed is the last gradient bucket, the first parameter gather, and any collective on the critical path that cannot be chunked.

blocks.prompt: With `--overlap-grad-reduce` on and 8 microbatches per step, when does the first gradient reduce-scatter start?
blocks.reveal: During the backward pass of the **8th** microbatch, as soon as the bucket holding the last layers is complete. For microbatches 1 to 7 the gradients only accumulate locally: reducing them earlier would send partial sums 8 times instead of the final sum once. This is also why a pipeline's last microbatch carries all the DP traffic.

blocks.question: A run with the distributed optimizer and d = 8 data-parallel ranks enables `--overlap-param-gather`. What exactly is overlapped with what?
options: The gradient reduce-scatter with the optimizer step
The all-gather of layer i+1's updated weights with the forward computation of layer i
The pipeline sends with the attention kernels
The Adam update of one shard with the Adam update of another
blocks.explain: After the optimizer step each rank has updated only its 1/8 shard, so the full BF16 weights must be all-gathered before use. The flag prefetches the next bucket's gather while the current layers compute. Gradient overlap is the separate --overlap-grad-reduce.

lessons.title: Mixture of experts at scale: EP, token dispatch and parallel folding

blocks.md:
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces the MLP with many expert MLPs and a router that sends each token to its top $k$. The *Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing* course covers routing, balancing losses and the basic expert-parallel all-to-all (its lessons 4, 5 and 8). This lesson follows one MoE layer through Megatron Core's code path and counts what it costs.

Tiny example first: 4 tokens on GPU 0, top-1 routing, experts 0-1 on GPU 0 and experts 2-3 on GPU 1. If tokens a and c choose expert 2, they must travel to GPU 1, be processed there, and come back before the next attention layer. That round trip, for every token and every MoE layer, is what expert parallelism (EP) adds.

blocks.title: One MoE layer in Megatron Core with expert parallelism

scenes.caption: Each GPU holds a different slice of the tokens. The router scores them and picks top-k experts per token (the routing math is in the fine-grained MoE course).
Permute: copies of each token are reordered so that tokens bound for the same expert are contiguous, one block per destination GPU.
Dispatch: an all-to-all sends every block to the GPU that owns its expert. Each GPU sends different data to every other GPU in its EP group.
Expert compute: each GPU runs all its local experts in one grouped GEMM (--moe-grouped-gemm), each expert on however many tokens it received.
Combine: a second all-to-all returns outputs to the GPUs the tokens came from; unpermute restores token order and sums each token's k outputs weighted by router probabilities.

blocks.md:
The token dispatcher (`--moe-token-dispatcher-type`) decides how tokens travel:

- `alltoall`: an all-to-all through NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, which runs Megatron's GPU collectives), the standard choice when EP is above 1.
- `allgather`: every GPU gathers all tokens instead of routing them, and keeps the ones its experts need; the guide suggests it for TP-only setups, small EP or large top-k.
- `flex` with `--moe-flex-dispatcher-backend deepep`: DeepSeek's DeepEP kernels, which remove redundant copies of a token crossing nodes and fuse the NVLink and InfiniBand stages into one kernel; recommended for cross-node EP and fine-grained MoE. The `hybridep` backend targets multi-node NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72.

Permutation and router kernels can be fused (`--moe-permute-fusion`, `--moe-router-fusion`), and the guide recommends keeping router logits in FP32 (`--moe-router-dtype fp32`) when there are many experts.

**How much traffic?** Take a DeepSeek-V3-like layer: hidden size 7168, top-8 of 256 routed experts, EP = 64 (V3 trained with 64-way EP spanning 8 nodes). A token is copied to 8 experts; with experts spread over 64 GPUs about 63/64 of the copies leave the GPU. Dispatch in BF16 is $8 \times 7168 \times 2 \times 63/64$ = 112.9 KB per token per layer, and the combine sends the same back. Compare a dense layer with TP = 8: two all-reduces of $2 \cdot \tfrac{7}{8} \cdot 7168 \cdot 2$ bytes = 50.2 KB per token. The bigger difference is the link: TP = 8 stays inside a server, while EP = 64 crosses the network. DeepSeek reports a computation-to-communication ratio of about 1:1 for this layout.

blocks.title: Bytes moved per token per layer, forward pass (h = 7168)

scenes.caption: A dense layer with TP = 8 sends 2 all-reduces x 2(7/8) x 7168 x 2 bytes = 50.2 KB per token per GPU, all inside one NVLink server.
Top-8 routing over EP = 64: 8 copies of the 7168-value hidden vector, 63/64 of them to another GPU, is 112.9 KB in BF16, and EP = 64 spans 8 servers.

DeepSeek-V3 dispatches in FP8 (56.4 KB plus small scale factors) and keeps the combine in BF16. Simplified: deduplicating dispatchers such as DeepEP send a token across the network once per destination node, not once per expert.

blocks.md:
**Load imbalance.** Dispatch and combine are collectives, so the layer finishes only when the busiest GPU does. One hot expert makes its GPU receive and compute more tokens while every other GPU waits at the combine. Balancing is set with `--moe-router-load-balancing-type` (`aux_loss`, `seq_aux_loss`, `global_aux_loss`, `sinkhorn`, `quantile_balancing` or `none`, plus `--moe-aux-loss-coeff`) or with aux-loss-free balancing, `--moe-router-enable-expert-bias` with `--moe-router-bias-update-rate` (default 1e-3, the DeepSeek-V3 value), which nudges a per-expert bias after each global batch.

A **capacity factor** caps tokens per expert: `--moe-expert-capacity-factor` (unset means dropless), with `--moe-token-drop-policy probs` dropping the lowest-probability tokens or `position` dropping the last ones. `--moe-pad-expert-input-to-capacity` pads every expert to the cap, giving static shapes that CUDA graphs (a recorded sequence of kernel launches replayed with one launch, which needs fixed tensor shapes) can capture.

blocks.title: Token copies received per GPU, EP = 8, one expert per GPU

scenes.caption: 1,024 token copies, perfectly balanced: every GPU receives 128 and its expert GEMM takes the same time.
Same 1,024 copies, but expert 3 is popular: GPU 3 receives 256. Its dispatch receive and its GEMM take twice as long (simplified model: time proportional to tokens).
The combine all-to-all cannot finish until GPU 3 returns its outputs, so all 8 GPUs wait: the layer runs at the pace of the hottest expert, about 2x here.

blocks.md:
**MoE parallel folding.** Attention and MoE layers want different splits. High TP suits attention but makes each expert's GEMM tiny; CP suits long attention but MoE layers treat tokens independently. Older frameworks also forced the EP group to sit inside the DP group, so EP could never exceed DP. Folding gives MoE layers their own four axes over the same GPUs: attention uses TP x CP x DP x PP, MoE uses ETP x EP x EDP x PP (expert TP, EP, expert DP), with only PP shared.

The docs' example: attention with TP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 8, PP = 4 could use at most EP = 8 before; folded, the MoE layers run ETP = 1, EP = 64, EDP = 1. And CP = 8 with EP = 8 no longer needs 64 GPUs; the two fold onto the same 8. In an MoE layer with ETP, the dispatcher adds an AllGather-V and a ReduceScatter-V inside each ETP group around the expert GEMM.

blocks.title: MoE parallel folding on 8 GPUs: two group maps

scenes.caption: Attention with TP = 2, CP = 2, DP = 2. TP varies fastest, so TP pairs are neighbours (0,1), (2,3) and so on.
CP pairs are (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7) and DP pairs (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7). Without folding, EP must sit inside DP, so EP could be at most 2.
With folding the MoE layers regroup the same 8 GPUs as ETP = 1, EP = 8, EDP = 1: each GPU owns 2 of 16 experts, and the all-to-all stays inside one NVLink server.

blocks.md:
**Hiding the all-to-all.** The docs say EP all-to-all can take 30 to 40% of step time without optimization. `--overlap-moe-expert-parallel-comm` with `--delay-wgrad-compute` merges the forward of one microbatch with the backward of another so one's all-to-all runs under the other's compute (needs EP above 1 and `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS` above 1); `--moe-shared-expert-overlap` runs the shared expert during the dispatch.

Placement rules from the MoE guide: keep EP x TP inside one NVLink domain, use PP to scale across nodes, prefer EP over expert TP (Mixtral 8x7B runs faster with EP = 8, TP = 1 than EP = 4, TP = 2), and enable `--sequence-parallel` whenever TP and EP are combined. For DeepSeek-V3-sized models whose EP must leave the node, use the all-to-all overlap. The parallelism guide's DeepSeek-V3 recipe uses 1,024 GPUs with TP = 2, PP = 16, EP = 64.

What it buys: the MoE Parallel Folding paper (BF16, H100) reports 49.3% MFU for Mixtral 8x22B and 39.0% for Qwen2-57B-A14B with folding, the best of the strategies it compared, while plain FSDP stayed below 10%. These are NVIDIA's measurements, not run here.

An MoE layer is route, permute, all-to-all dispatch, grouped GEMM, all-to-all combine, unpermute. Its cost is set by bytes per token times the slowest link in the EP group, and by the hottest expert. Folding lets MoE layers choose EP freely while attention keeps its own TP and CP.

blocks.question: A team moves an MoE model from EP = 8 inside one 8-GPU server to EP = 16 across two servers, keeping everything else the same. Which part of the step grows most, and why?
options: The expert GEMMs, because each GPU now holds twice as many experts
The router, because it must score twice as many experts
The dispatch and combine all-to-alls, because about half of each token's expert copies now cross the slower inter-node network
Nothing, the all-to-all volume per GPU is unchanged
blocks.explain: With 16 ranks over 2 servers, about 8/16 of a token's experts live on the other server, so roughly half the dispatch and combine bytes leave NVLink for the network, which is many times slower. Each GPU holds fewer experts, not more. This is why the guide keeps EP x TP inside the NVLink domain and uses PP across nodes.

blocks.question: Attention runs with TP = 2, CP = 2, DP = 2 on 8 GPUs. Without folding, EP must live inside the DP group. What is the largest EP without and with MoE parallel folding?
options: 2 without folding, 8 with folding
8 in both cases
4 without folding, 4 with folding
2 in both cases, since folding only changes TP
blocks.explain: Without folding the expert group is a subgroup of DP, so EP is at most DP = 2. Folding lets the MoE layers regroup all 8 GPUs (ETP x EP x EDP = 8 per pipeline stage), so EP = 8 with ETP = 1 and EDP = 1 is allowed.

lessons.title: FP8 training with Transformer Engine in Megatron Core

blocks.md:
Precision is a performance knob. NVIDIA's H100 SXM spec lists 1,979 TFLOP/s for BF16 tensor cores and 3,958 for FP8, both with sparsity; dense, that is about 989 and 1,979. So FP8 matrix multiplies can run up to twice as fast, and FP8 tensors are half the bytes to store and send.

In brief (the *FP8 and FP4 training* course, outside this course's prerequisites, covers it in depth): E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) reaches 448, E5M2 reaches 57,344 with less precision, and a per-tensor or per-block **scale** slides values into that window. For example, a tensor whose largest magnitude is 0.02 is multiplied by 448 / 0.02 = 22,400 before the cast and divided by it again after the GEMM; unscaled, values below about 0.001 would round to zero, since E4M3's smallest nonzero value is about 0.002. The FP8 Formats paper recommends E4M3 for weights and activations and E5M2 for gradients. In Megatron Core the FP8 kernels come from NVIDIA's Transformer Engine (TE); `--fp8-format e4m3` uses E4M3 everywhere and `--fp8-format hybrid` uses E4M3 forward and E5M2 for activation gradients.

**Recipes.** The hardware below is NVIDIA GPU generations: Hopper (H100, H200), Ada (L4, L40S) and Blackwell (B200, GB200). `--fp8-recipe` picks how scales are computed; FP4 uses `--fp4-format e2m1` instead, and FP8 and FP4 cannot both be on:

- `delayed` (default): scale from a rolling amax (largest absolute value) history, `--fp8-amax-history-len`. Hopper, Ada, Blackwell. The only recipe that works with optimizer CPU offload.
- `tensorwise`: current scaling from the tensor itself, no history; avoids the early-training warm-up issues of delayed.
- `blockwise`: 1 x 128 activation blocks and 128 x 128 weight blocks (DeepSeek-V3 style), Hopper and Blackwell; the MoE guide's production recommendation on Hopper.
- `mxfp8`: power-of-two scale per 1 x 32 block, Blackwell only.
- `nvfp4` (via `--fp4-recipe`): FP4 with 16-value blocks, Blackwell, Transformer Engine 2.7.0.dev0 or newer.

blocks.title: Which values share one scale factor, per recipe (schematic)

scenes.caption: Two rows of an activation tensor, each cell standing for 16 values. delayed and tensorwise: one scale for the whole tensor (delayed takes it from an amax history, tensorwise from the current tensor).
blockwise (DeepSeek-style): one scale per 1 x 128 block of activations (128 x 128 for weights), so each token row gets its own scale and one outlier row cannot squash the others.
mxfp8 (Blackwell): one power-of-two scale per 1 x 32 block, 4 scales per row. Finer blocks follow local magnitudes more closely.
nvfp4 (Blackwell, 4-bit E2M1 values): one scale per 16 values, 8 scales per row, plus a tensor-wide scale. Details of every recipe are in the FP8 and FP4 training course.

blocks.md: **What stays in high precision.** The optimizer always steps on FP32 main weights, and Adam's moments stay FP32 unless `--use-precision-aware-optimizer` with `--exp-avg-dtype` and `--exp-avg-sq-dtype` lowers them (to BF16, FP16 or FP8). `--first-last-layers-bf16` keeps the first and last transformer blocks in BF16 (`--num-layers-at-start-in-bf16` and `--num-layers-at-end-in-bf16`, default 1 each; the docs suggest 2 to 4 for FP4 or very deep models), the first defense against early loss spikes. Other levers: `--fp8-margin` adds headroom to the scale, and turning off `--fp8-wgrad` keeps the weight-gradient GEMM in higher precision.

**Communication.** `--fp8-param-gather` keeps the parameters in FP8 and runs the distributed optimizer's parameter all-gather in FP8, halving it (the MoE guide excepts MXFP8 from this saving). It requires the distributed optimizer, Torch FSDP2 or Megatron-FSDP (Megatron rejects it at startup otherwise), and with `mxfp8` the docs pair it with `--reuse-grad-buf-for-mxfp8-param-ag` (Megatron warns of extra memory without it). For MoE, FP8 dispatch halves the EP dispatch volume, and `--moe-router-padding-for-fp8` pads the routing map so expert inputs meet FP8 GEMM alignment. The MoE guide also lists halving the stored inputs of linear layers as an activation-memory saving.

blocks.title: Parameter all-gather per step, 70B model sharded TP x PP = 16

scenes.caption: Each model shard holds 70.6B / 16 = 4.41B parameters. With the distributed optimizer, the BF16 all-gather rebuilds these 8.82 GB of weights each step (each GPU receives 3/4 of it at DP x CP = 4).
Keeping the parameters in FP8 and gathering them in FP8 halves this to 4.41 GB, the 50% the MoE guide quotes. EP dispatch in FP8 halves that traffic the same way.

blocks.code:
# Hopper / H100, fastest stable FP8 (docs cookbook)
--bf16 --fp8-format hybrid --fp8-recipe tensorwise \
--fp8-param-gather --use-distributed-optimizer

# Hopper, DeepSeek-style blockwise (MoE guide, production)
--fp8-format e4m3 --fp8-recipe blockwise \
--fp8-param-gather --moe-router-padding-for-fp8

# Blackwell / B200
--bf16 --fp8-format e4m3 --fp8-recipe mxfp8 --fp8-param-gather \
--reuse-grad-buf-for-mxfp8-param-ag --use-distributed-optimizer

# Blackwell, FP4
--bf16 --fp4-format e2m1 --fp4-param-gather --first-last-layers-bf16 \
--num-layers-at-start-in-bf16 2 --num-layers-at-end-in-bf16 2 \
--use-distributed-optimizer
blocks.caption: Starting points from the Megatron Core low-precision guide and MoE guide. Not run here: there is no Hopper or Blackwell GPU on this machine.

blocks.md: **FP8 and MFU.** MFU divides achieved model FLOPs by a peak, and with FP8 there are two peaks. Llama 3's report is explicit: it quotes "BF16 MFU" of 38 to 43%. Suppose a run reaches 45% MFU in BF16 and FP8 makes it 1.3x faster. Against the BF16 peak (989 TFLOP/s) that is 58.5%; against the FP8 peak (1,979) it is about 29%. Both are honest only if the denominator is named, and only same-denominator numbers can be compared. The speedup is also well below 2x because only the GEMMs got faster (Amdahl's law: the overall speedup is capped by the share of time that did not get faster; the FP8 course's lesson 4 works through it).

Mismatched recipes fail quietly. For a run that converges slower than its BF16 baseline, the low-precision guide's first check is that the recipe matches the hardware table, because a mismatched recipe silently falls back to slower paths.

blocks.question: A team switches a run from BF16 to FP8 and the reported MFU jumps from 45% to 58.5%. Throughput rose 1.3x. What should a reviewer check first?
options: Whether the FP8 run silently enabled activation recomputation
Whether the MFU is still divided by the BF16 peak; against the FP8 peak the same run is about 29%
Whether the tokenizer changed, since MFU depends on vocabulary size
Nothing; MFU always rises by the speedup factor
blocks.explain: 45% x 1.3 = 58.5% only if the denominator stayed at the BF16 peak. FP8 doubles the dense peak, so against it the run is at about 29%. Neither number is wrong, but a report must name which peak it uses, as Llama 3 does with its BF16 MFU.

blocks.question: An H100 run needs FP8 together with optimizer CPU offload. Which recipe does Megatron Core accept?
options: tensorwise
blockwise
delayed
mxfp8
blocks.explain: The low-precision guide states that only delayed scaling is supported with optimizer CPU offload, and Megatron enforces it in its argument checks. mxfp8 also needs Blackwell.

lessons.title: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count

blocks.md: **Measuring the result.** PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022, the paper behind Google's 540-billion-parameter PaLM model) defined **model FLOPs utilization (MFU)**: observed tokens per second divided by the tokens per second the hardware could process at peak FLOP/s. Only FLOPs the *model* requires count. A dense decoder with $N$ parameters needs $6N$ matmul FLOPs per token (2N forward, 4N backward). Each parameter does one multiply and one add per token in the forward pass, 2N FLOPs; the backward pass computes gradients for both the activations and the weights, each as costly as the forward, 4N.

Attention adds $12LHQT$ ($L$ layers, $H$ heads, head size $Q$, sequence length $T$), because its score and weighted-sum matmuls use no parameters: per token and layer each costs $2HQT$ FLOPs forward, $4LHQT$ over all layers, and times 3 for forward plus backward gives $12LHQT$. Recomputation is *not* counted, so MFU cannot be gamed by doing extra work. **Hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU)** counts everything the GPU actually executed, recompute included.

blocks.caption: In words: tokens per second times the model's FLOPs per token, divided by what all the GPUs could do together at peak.

blocks.md:
Worked example: the 530B GPT model (105 layers, $h$ = 20480, 128 heads, $s$ = 2048) from Korthikanti et al., on 280 A100s (peak 312 TFLOP/s BF16) with TP = 8, PP = 35, batch 280 sequences, measured at 37.83 s per iteration.

1. Tokens per second: 280 x 2048 / 37.83 = 15,158.
2. $6N$ part: 15,158 x 6 x 529.6e9 / (280 x 312e12) = 55.1%.
3. Attention part: $12 \cdot 105 \cdot 128 \cdot 160 \cdot 2048$ FLOPs (head size 20480 / 128 = 160) per token adds 0.9%.
4. **MFU = 56.0%**, matching the paper. The paper's HFU of 57.0% uses its Equation 8, which counts the recompute generously; adding only the $4bs^2h$ recomputed FLOPs per layer gives about 56.3%. Scaling to 8-way DP (2,240 GPUs, 39.15 s) gives 54.2%.

Where the 72 and 96 in the next figure come from: Narayanan et al. count $24bsh^2$ matmul FLOPs per layer per forward pass (lesson 4). Forward plus backward is 3 times that, $72bsh^2$; full recompute adds a fourth forward pass, $96bsh^2$. So removing the recompute scales their number by 72/96 = 0.75.

blocks.title: Same hardware counter, different stories: HFU vs MFU

scenes.caption: Narayanan et al.'s 1T model: 163 TFLOP/s per GPU = 52.2% of 312, counted with full recompute (96 instead of 72 in the FLOP formula). Dropping the recompute FLOPs gives an MFU of about 39.2%.
Korthikanti et al.'s 530B run with SP + selective recompute: HFU 57.0% and MFU 56.0%. Almost no wasted FLOPs, so the two metrics nearly agree, and true speed is far higher.

For comparison PaLM computes the production Megatron-Turing NLG (MT-NLG, NLG for natural language generation) 530B run (65.43K tokens/s on 2,240 A100s) at about 30.2% MFU, and PaLM 540B at 46.2% MFU with 57.8% HFU.

blocks.md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization (another name for recomputation).

Reference points from the H100 benchmarks in the Megatron-LM README (present in the README of release core_v0.20.1; the main-branch README no longer lists them): up to **47% MFU** on H100 clusters, rising from 41% for the smallest benchmarked model to 47 to 48% for the largest because bigger GEMMs are more efficient, and falling from 47% to 42% when strong-scaling (adding GPUs while the total batch stays fixed) GPT-3 175B from 96 to 4,608 GPUs at a fixed batch of 1,152 sequences, as communication becomes exposed.

The Megatron Core guide's order for choosing a configuration: start with DP (plus the distributed optimizer), add TP inside a node if the model does not fit, add PP across nodes for very large models, add CP for long sequences, and use activation recompute or offload (moving activations to CPU memory) only in extreme cases.
Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

blocks.prompt: A run reports 50% 'GPU utilization' using full activation recomputation. Roughly what MFU should you expect, ignoring attention and logits?
blocks.reveal: About 37.5%. Full recompute adds one extra forward pass: per token the hardware does 2N (forward) + 2N (recomputed forward) + 4N (backward) = 8N FLOPs instead of 6N. MFU = HFU x 6/8 = 50% x 0.75 = 37.5%. The 1T example above shows the same 72/96 ratio: 52.2% becomes about 39%.

blocks.question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
blocks.explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

blocks.question: Two runs of the same model on the same GPUs both report 160 TFLOP/s per GPU. Run A uses full recompute, run B uses selective recompute. Which trains faster in tokens per second?
options: Run A, because full recompute frees memory for larger batches
They are the same, the TFLOP/s are equal
Run B, because fewer of its FLOPs are wasted on recomputation, so more go to useful model FLOPs
It cannot be decided without knowing the vocabulary size
blocks.explain: Both execute FLOPs at the same rate, but A spends about a quarter of them redoing the forward pass. B's model FLOPs per second, and so its MFU and tokens per second, are higher. This is exactly the HFU vs MFU distinction.

lessons.title: Hands on: plan, launch, profile and checkpoint an MCore run

blocks.md: Time to use everything at once. The job: a Llama-3-70B-like dense model (80 layers, hidden size 8192, 64 query heads with 8 KV heads, SwiGLU MLP of 28,672 (a gated MLP with three weight matrices, gate, up and down, instead of two), 128,000-token vocabulary, 70.6B parameters), 8K-token sequences, a global batch of 512 sequences, on 64 H100 80 GB GPUs in 8 servers. Four steps: plan the layout on paper, launch it, measure and profile it, and checkpoint it so a failure or a cluster change costs minutes, not days.

**1. Plan.** For each candidate layout compute, for the first pipeline stage (the fullest one):

- Model state with the distributed optimizer: $(6 + 12/(\text{DP} \cdot \text{CP}))$ bytes per parameter, times the parameters on one GPU, about $N/(\text{TP} \cdot \text{PP})$. The optimizer shards over DP and CP together, because CP ranks hold the same weights.
- Activations: with SP and fused attention, $34\,sbh/(\text{TP} \cdot \text{CP})$ bytes per layer, and 1F1B puts $L$ layers' worth on stage 1 (lesson 4).
- Bubble: $(p-1)/m$ with $m$ = global batch / (micro-batch x DP).

This is a simplified model: it uses the GPT activation constant for a SwiGLU, grouped-query model and ignores logits, buffers and fragmentation, so keep a margin.

blocks.code:
L, h, ffn, kvh, hd, V, s, b, GBS = 80, 8192, 28672, 8, 128, 128000, 8192, 1, 512
layer = 2*h*h + 2*h*kvh*hd + 3*h*ffn
N = L*layer + 2*h*V
print("params %.2fB per-layer %.1fM" % (N/1e9, layer/1e6))
def plan(tp, pp, cp, dp):
    assert tp*pp*cp*dp == 64
    state = (6 + 12/(dp*cp)) * N/(tp*pp) / 1e9
    act_layer = 34*s*b*h/(tp*cp) / 1e9
    act = L * act_layer          # 1F1B stage 0 holds p microbatches x L/p layers
    m = GBS // (b*dp)
    bubble = (pp-1)/m
    return state, act_layer, act, state+act, m, bubble
for cfg in [(4,4,2,2),(8,1,1,8),(4,8,1,2),(8,2,1,4)]:
    st, al, a, tot, m, bub = plan(*cfg)
    print("TP%d PP%d CP%d DP%d: state %.1f GB, act/layer %.3f GB, act %.1f GB, total %.1f GB, m=%d bubble %.2f%%" % (*cfg, st, al, a, tot, m, 100*bub))
# Output:
# params 70.55B per-layer 855.6M
# TP4 PP4 CP2 DP2: state 39.7 GB, act/layer 0.285 GB, act 22.8 GB, total 62.5 GB, m=256 bubble 1.17%
# TP8 PP1 CP1 DP8: state 66.1 GB, act/layer 0.285 GB, act 22.8 GB, total 89.0 GB, m=64 bubble 0.00%
# TP4 PP8 CP1 DP2: state 26.5 GB, act/layer 0.570 GB, act 45.6 GB, total 72.1 GB, m=256 bubble 2.73%
# TP8 PP2 CP1 DP4: state 39.7 GB, act/layer 0.285 GB, act 22.8 GB, total 62.5 GB, m=128 bubble 0.78%
